title: SEO Is DEAD In 2025! (Here's What You Should Do Instead) | Eric Siu
speakers_and_attribution: Adam Robinson hosts; Eric Siu is the principal guest and identifies Single Grain, Marketing School and Leveling Up as his businesses/media projects. Santos participates as a co-host and describes prior work at ZoomInfo; his surname is not established here. An opening participant, addressed inconsistently as Gary/Jerry, discusses an analytics service. Ashley, introduced as Ashley Bass and self-captioned as Ashley Basson, briefly discusses product marketing and community development. Captions are not diarized, so attribution follows introductions, direct address and conversational continuity. Eric's agency results, tools, community, investments and client examples are not Adam's achievements. Several short interjections remain uncertain. Opening and closing excerpts repeat material from the main conversation.
summary: The conversation argues that SEO is evolving into discovery across multiple platforms, while remaining a potentially valuable long-term investment. Eric recommends sequencing SEO after product-market fit and a working acquisition channel, using human-reviewed AI workflows, and treating communities as products requiring customer development. Adam contributes substantive context about his audience near $1 million ARR, the early design of his paid founder community, LinkedIn as an existing community, and an RB2B plateau he associates with stopping customer discovery while competitors emerged. Later sections cover Eric's company-personalized LinkedIn advertising tool, community segmentation, channel concentration risk and the staffing economics of content repurposing. The title's claim that SEO is dead is not supported by the spoken discussion.

key_learnings.claim: Eric frames modern SEO as search everywhere optimization: content and links still matter, but discovery also happens through YouTube, Amazon and AI products, requiring attention to where people actually search.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Guest framework, not Adam's established strategy. Eric also says Google remains dominant; he does not claim conventional search has disappeared.

key_learnings.claim: For a resource-constrained startup around or below $1 million ARR, Eric recommends identifying and scaling the best-performing channel before attempting broad channel coverage.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: A stage-dependent resource-allocation heuristic, not a universal revenue cutoff or a claim that Adam's company was at this scale.

key_learnings.claim: Eric considers SEO a poor initial investment when a founder has little runway and has not raised capital, because returns may take a year or longer; he still regards it as a valuable compounding asset over time.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Guest advice conditioned on runway and payback timing. It does not establish a preference by Adam for or against venture funding.

key_learnings.claim: Eric's Marketing School workflow turns an in-person recording into audio, long-form video, short clips and AI-assisted blog posts; a human checks facts, links and statistics before the written material is used.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Eric reports consistently increasing podcast-site traffic but supplies no traffic series, attribution analysis or production cost for this workflow.

key_learnings.claim: Santos describes historical programmatic SEO at ZoomInfo using large numbers of person and company landing pages, then asks whether the approach remains viable with AI-generated content.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos
key_learnings.caveat: This is Santos's historical experience, approximately a decade before the conversation, not Adam's work or a present-day recommendation.

key_learnings.claim: Eric says Single Grain recovered programmatic SEO results after a Google update by deleting pages without traffic or backlinks and improving remaining content and calls to action at scale.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Self-reported recovery with no controlled attribution or numerical before-and-after traffic values. The update's identity and timing are not independently established.

key_learnings.claim: Eric acknowledges manipulative backlink tactics can work, but says his agency avoids them because of the risk of severe website losses; he prefers legitimate sites and relationships despite the additional work.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: His characterization of legitimate cross-linking is informal, not a verified statement of search-engine policy.

key_learnings.claim: Eric sees communities serving two purposes: generating discoverable human contributions and giving customers a reason to remain involved after purchase.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: The causal explanation linking AI content proliferation to search gains is Eric's interpretation. He discloses an investment in the platform captioned as School/Skool.

key_learnings.claim: Adam says the people his LinkedIn content helps most are around $1 million ARR, and identifies premature investment in cold email, advertising and other channels before product-market fit or a solid value proposition as a recurring problem.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: Adam's assessment of his audience and its problems at recording time; this is not a validated audience study or an approved mission statement.

key_learnings.claim: Eric recommends treating a new community like a product: choose a platform, hire an experienced community manager if resources allow, and keep the founder involved in energizing members and learning their problems during the early months.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Drawn from his Agency Owners Association experience. Hiring a manager does not remove his recommended early founder involvement.

key_learnings.claim: Eric distinguishes a private community that is not indexed from a free, public community intended to support discovery, and suggests a free-to-private progression for Adam.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Platform behavior is described by Eric as of the conversation. His own demonstrated group is private, and the suggested free community is not evidence that Adam implemented it.

key_learnings.claim: Adam's initial paid community combines startup courses, a year of a Pro product, introductions, founder habits, exclusive daily content and monthly training; a higher tier adds weekly access to his operating team.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: An early offer description, not evidence of sales, retention or validated outcomes. Captions are unclear on product spelling and the higher-tier price.

key_learnings.claim: Adam suspects the community has too many channels and creates choice paralysis; he is considering consolidating activity into one channel while he, Pete and power users sustain engagement.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: A diagnosis and proposed change around day 20, not a completed simplification or measured result.

key_learnings.claim: Eric recommends organizing community offers around the problems members face at different business stages, rather than adding more calls and activities without a clear customer need.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: His revenue-based segmentation and executive/M&A examples concern agency founders; the proposed event cadence is tentative.

key_learnings.claim: Adam says he and Santos did extensive customer development before launching RB2B but stopped doing it for roughly nine months; he associates the resulting plateau and customers turning off the product with new competition and an offering that no longer met needs.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: Adam's causal diagnosis, not independently demonstrated causation. He gives no numerical churn rate or plateau revenue.

key_learnings.claim: Adam concludes that customer conversations must continue as conditions change, and agrees that operating a community is effectively running another business.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: A lesson drawn from his reported lapse in customer discovery, not evidence that a replacement discovery process had already been installed.

key_learnings.claim: Eric chooses tools by channel and task: vidIQ for YouTube competitor and video performance analysis, and a tool captioned as HRS, alongside Semrush, for conventional SEO.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Historical guest preferences. HRS appears to be an automatic-caption rendering of Ahrefs, but the spelling cannot be verified from the supplied text.

key_learnings.claim: Eric designs AI agents by first defining a role's jobs to be done, then implementing bounded workflows such as fetching Search Console data, identifying similar content and preparing consolidation recommendations.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: His working model for agent design, not proof that the full SEO-manager role had been automated.

key_learnings.claim: Eric keeps humans responsible for reviewing agent recommendations and approving changes because he does not consider AI reliable enough to operate entirely unattended; he applies this to consolidation and internal linking.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: His estimate of two to three years until greater autonomy is a forecast from recording time. Several broader agent capabilities are roadmap intentions.

key_learnings.claim: Eric says a customer-side complaint about creating LinkedIn account campaigns individually led his team to build batch campaign creation with company-specific creative variables and ad copy.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Guest product-development account. Claims of unique market capability and LinkedIn confirmation are unverified reports.

key_learnings.claim: Eric used a LinkedIn demonstration post and a comment/message call to action to generate enterprise interest and sales conversations for the advertising tool.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Reported engagement and booked calls are top-of-funnel outcomes, not closed customers or revenue.

key_learnings.claim: Eric reports lower cost per click and higher target-account engagement for company-personalized ads, but says conversion-rate conclusions were premature because the sales cycle was long.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Early, guest-reported comparison without sample size, measurement window or experimental design.

key_learnings.claim: Eric declines to advise on entertainment-channel advertising RPM because his YouTube objective is generating leads for his business.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: A useful boundary on his expertise and success metric; it does not establish Adam's monetization model.

key_learnings.claim: Eric explains that his agency-owner community is strategically valuable as a source of potential partnerships and acquisitions, not simply as a subscription-revenue product.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Intent and acquisition screening logic; no completed acquisition attributable to the community is reported.

key_learnings.claim: Adam regards recurring LinkedIn discussion around shared ideas, including his replies to comments, as community building already; moving members to a dedicated platform is optional.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: Adam explicitly draws on an idea he attributes to Dave Gerhardt. His description does not resolve the risks of relying on a rented platform.

key_learnings.claim: Santos argues that niche communities can be sufficient for high-value businesses and that founders should not automatically optimize for a very large membership count.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos
key_learnings.caveat: His example of 300 members at $60,000 ACV is hypothetical and omits conversion and retention assumptions.

key_learnings.claim: Eric uses a self-improvement community as an example of a free audience feeding a paid membership, with additional tiers forming a progression of offers.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: An observed non-SaaS comparison, not Eric's or Adam's business. Displayed membership multiplied by price does not establish collected revenue or profitability.

key_learnings.claim: Eric favors AI-assisted content with substantial human contribution, arguing that a modest additional quality effort can differentiate content from low-effort automated publishing.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: The suggested AI/human split is a heuristic, not a measured productivity result. His long-term SEO argument remains conditioned by earlier runway concerns.

key_learnings.claim: Eric says starting SEO in 2025 is harder than a decade earlier and warns mature marketing operations against dependence on one platform that can change abruptly.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: This introduces tension with early-stage channel focus; the conversation supports sequencing diversification after establishing traction, rather than doing every channel immediately.

key_learnings.claim: When Adam asks for a practical readiness test, Eric recommends considering SEO once a company has product-market fit and at least one working acquisition channel.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Eric explicitly presents this as a simple, safe heuristic; he supplies no budget, runway or market-demand checklist.

key_learnings.claim: Eric treats repurposing as an ongoing distribution expense and describes a three-role production pod: someone selects moments, an editor creates clips, and a third person posts and schedules them.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Staffing and cost figures come from an unnamed operator's business. Eric suggests one or two pods may suffice for others; he does not promise equivalent reach.

key_learnings.claim: Eric says co-owned community operation remains an experiment for him and Neil through the Agency Owners Association, rather than offering an established successful example.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Siu
key_learnings.caveat: Explicit uncertainty about outcomes; the community's existence is not evidence that joint ownership has been validated.

tensions_and_corrections: The sensational title says SEO is dead; Eric repeatedly says content, links and Google remain important and recommends SEO under suitable conditions.
Early-stage focus and later diversification are both advocated. Preserve the sequencing: concentrate scarce resources until one channel works, then reduce dependence on a single platform.

Community SEO benefits require discoverable content. Eric's demonstrated Agency Owners Association is private and explicitly not indexed, so its retention and acquisition-sourcing benefits do not establish SEO benefits for that group.
Adam initially wanted RB2B to be community-led, but says the specific audience and offer took about nine months to clarify. Strategic intent preceded a concrete community design.

Adam reports extensive prelaunch discovery followed by about nine months without it. His later insistence on continuous customer conversations reflects a lesson from a lapse, not an uninterrupted practice.
Adam describes the advertising tool as hyper-personalized; Eric qualifies that description and says it personalizes at the company level. Individual-level personalization is not established.
ABM engagement and CPC improvements are early indicators. Eric explicitly says conversion results are not yet available because the sales cycle is long.
Eric's statements that nobody else can provide the batch LinkedIn functionality, including his account of LinkedIn's response, are promotional claims without independent verification.
Community pricing is unreliable in captions: 997 for the entry bundle and 29.97 for the higher tier. Currency, decimal placement and billing period require verification before reuse.
Diana's sales history changes from $1 million to $10 million twice to zero to $10 million ARR twice. Preserve both versions; neither establishes that Adam personally achieved these sales results.
The current role-poll percentages total 98%. The source does not explain the missing two percentage points.
At 00:01:34 the caption says 3:46 in an attendance-related exchange; it may mean 346, but the text is insufficient to treat it as a reliable additional attendance metric.

The question about communities for companies that are not already scaled is only partly answered: Adam uses a roughly $25 million ARR company, Santos offers a hypothetical small niche community, and Eric shows a large non-SaaS community.
An audience question asks for an ACV threshold, but Eric answers using prospective member-company revenue. These units are not interchangeable.
Eric's agent platform includes a shown internal-linking workflow and broader planned capabilities. Do not describe every mentioned marketing agent as already shipped or fully autonomous.
Eric forecasts greater AI reliability in two to three years while recommending human review at the time of recording. This is a dated prediction, not a current capability assessment.
Eric promises an advanced SEO authority-building discussion for funded companies around 00:19:41, but no distinct completed explanation of that promised tactic appears later.
Adam initially assumes Ashley wants business referrals; she clarifies that community advice is not her side business, and he acknowledges the misreading.
The third-party paid-community revenue is inferred from displayed membership and price. It should not be treated as verified collected revenue, recurring revenue quality or profit.
